correctness.rationale: Angular orthogonality in the target measure gives positive diagonal coefficients u^n∫_0^x t^n e^(−t)dt/n!=u^n q_n(x); factorial tail bounds give every positive Schatten exponent and positivity gives injectivity. Writing p_k for the Poisson masses, q_n/p_{n+1} is 1 plus a sum of strictly decreasing positive terms in n and tends to 1, so q_{n+1}/q_n decreases strictly to 0. It follows that only a single degree or two adjacent degrees maximize. At a tie the norm-attaining vectors form the span of the two normalized monomials, not just two lines. The ratio q_0/q_1 gives the exact first threshold and its stated expansion. Independently, if p'_k is the mass of Pois(ux), then e^{−x(u−1)}a_n=Σ_{j≥1}u^{−j}p'_{n+j}. The largest Poisson mass is asymptotic to (2πux)^(−1/2); this supplies an upper bound multiplied by Σ_{j≥1}u^{−j}=1/(u−1). Taking n=floor(ux), each fixed j attains the same leading mass, and geometric domination gives the matching lower bound. For n≥(u+ε)x all terms have exponentially small masses. For n≤(u−ε)x the terms with j≤εx/2 have exponentially small masses and the remaining geometric tail is exponentially small. Thus every maximizing n_x/x tends to u, with no lattice prefactor. The displayed radial Toeplitz symbol has the same coefficients by rescaling the radial integral.
residual_risks: Fixed u>1 only in the large-radius asymptotic; not a joint near-threshold limit. The full list is indexed by degree, not by decreasing magnitude.

value.rationale: A concentric cutoff is a natural regularization of an otherwise unbounded cross-weight inclusion. The exponentially small first transition interval, exact neighboring-degree thresholds and the nontrivial power and coefficient multiplying the fixed-mismatch exponential distinguish the behavior of its worst mode. These are useful sharp data beyond a known diagonalization or exponential-order estimate.
residual_risks: The theorem does not interpolate uniformly between the first threshold and fixed mismatch or treat nonradial cutoffs.
